utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the Registry, counsel for the Prosecution and for the Defence. We shall now resume our proceedings. It is Mr. Krstan Simic's turn, and I give him the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. The Defence calls Witness Pero Rendic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pero Rendic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please approach the microphones. Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming. First you will be answering questions put to you by Mr. Krstan Simic. Krstan Simic, your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, as you know, my name is Krstan Simic. I am an attorney from Banja Luka, and together with Mr. Branko Lukic, an attorney from Doboj, we are representing Mr. Kvocka in this case. In that context, I will have a number of questions for you, but I would like to ask you to be kind enough to wait a few moments after hearing my question before giving your answers so that we do not overlap and cause unnecessary difficulties for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Rendic, will you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Pero Rendic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Rendic?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of September, 1948.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: In the village of Maricka, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you reside now?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: In Omarska. Prvomajska Street 139.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, what is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I graduated from secondary school in Prijedor in 1966. In 1972, I completed a two-year post-secondary education in Banja Luka. It is the secondary school of catering, and I started working in that field and continued until 1987.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you do now?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I have my own private catering establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: In Omarska. Brace Mitrovic street, no number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you completed your obligatory military service in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: In March 1967, I started my military service in the Republic of Croatia, in the town of Solin. I spent six months there in the recruiting centre. After that, I went on to Split where I served the rest of my military service, and in June 1968 I was discharged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is a mistake in the transcript. You said you were discharged. It's written here --

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me explain. There was a crisis in Czechoslovakia, and as I was entitled to a holiday, so I left the army a little earlier. I don't remember the exact dates, but I can tell you the month and the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing your military service in the JNA, were you registered in the military records of military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had to report immediately to the National Defence Department in Prijedor, and I was given a military assignment which was written into my military booklet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, what is a military conscript after a person has completed his military service?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: A military conscript is a person who is over 18 years of age and who until the age of 60 in peacetime and in wartime, is duty-bound to respond to all call-ups sent by the ministry to an able-bodied military conscript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, our interest focuses on 1992, so I would like to ask you, in the course of that year, 1992, were you mobilised under a regular procedure?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: May I say something before answering that question? As I was a non-commissioned officer of the JNA, so ever since I had left the army, 1968 until 1986, I was a member of regular JN units, which means a member of the 43rd Motorised Brigade. Because I went through so many reserve trainings and regular reserve training every two years in Vinkovci, I was, in a sense, released from the unit and transferred to the Territorial Defence of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, will you explain what the TO of Omarska means?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: It is also a unit with fewer personnel which is not engaged in the same way as regular reserve units in the 43rd Motorised Brigade. They act as civil defence for the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you roughly remember when it was that you were transferred from the motorised brigade to the Omarska Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid not with precision. It is difficult to remember all the dates in one's life so I find it difficult to pinpoint that particular date, but I think it was in 1986, around the month of May. Please don't hold me by my word. It is really difficult for one to remember all those details. After all, it was all a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, as of 1986 approximately, you were a member of the detachment of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: It was not a detachment, it was a platoon. A detachment is slightly larger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional information, but let us go back to my original question. Were you mobilised and in what month of 1992, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Let me try. Let me go back a little further. As in those days, I had my own private business together with my wife. We had a lot to do because of that business. So I was mobilised, I think it was the beginning of May. Again, I can't remember the exact date, but anyway, allow me to explain how I was mobilised later on, or actually, how it came about that I performed the duties that I did in the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, as a member of the unit to which you mobilised in May 1992, what was your specific assignment in that unit?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: As I am a logistics man in the regular 43rd Motorised Brigade, I was leader of the Quatermaster's Unit. Later on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Mr. Rendic, to make it quite clear for Their Honours and the rest of us here, could you please tell us what is a Quartermaster's section, how many men it consists of, and what its assignments are. Be as brief and precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: A Quartermaster's Detachment consists of 12 men. Most are cooks, tailors, and such like, everything that is required to provide a soldier from his clothes to the preparation of food. Is that a good explanation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. What particular duty did you have within that Quatermaster's Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: That brings me back to your previous question. As I had worked in a private catering establishment and being aware of my organisational abilities, the commander came up to me and told me, "Pero, put a uniform on for a while and go to the mines and take over the kitchen operating under wartime conditions." I went there. I found the personnel, the women working there, the manager of the kitchen, Dusko he was called. I explained to him what I had come to do, that I had been assigned to prepare food for the troops or, rather, to organise the preparation of food. The first time I encountered the personnel of the mine and their abilities told me that this personnel, together with me, would not be able to carry out the tasks assigned us to in the way that I thought would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that this task was assigned to you by the assistant commander for logistics within the Omarska territorial unit. Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Mr. Milan Andzic, who was the Acting Assistant Commander for Logistics, and he was the one who could issue me orders, and he probably received orders from the battalion commander and they from the Crisis Staff, but I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, to round it off, this section regarding the command of the territorial unit, you told us that you were squad leader, your assistant commander was Mr. Andzic, and who was the commander of this Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Rane Radanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, you mentioned the fact that in May and the month that followed, as the leader of the Quartermaster Squad, you prepared food for the soldiers. Before we go on to the next set of questions, would you be kind enough to very briefly explain to Their Honours the composition of the personnel involved in food preparation?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I have already said that once I had met the mine personnel, I realised that they would not be able to accomplish the tasks assigned to us. I looked for a man who would be a professional cook, also a professional butcher, so that together with me, because I was the one organising these activities, to be able to carry out the tasks assigned to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to you, a butcher, and a cook, were there other army members in this squad involved in food preparation?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, no one else. The rest were just women workers, the cooks from the iron ore mine who were under work obligation. There were between 12 and 15 of them. It depended on the number that the manager assigned to the kitchen for that day rather than depending on the kind of meal that was being prepared for the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, in addition to these women employed in the Ljubija or Omarska mines, this Quartermaster Squad, in the course of its work, was it assisted by other persons, and if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were other persons. There were persons also from the catering field, from the Omarska agricultural cooperative, their kitchen there, from catering facilities where their wives were cooks. So in answer to your question, there were other civilians who came to assist us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, let us go back to the managerial structure within that Quartermaster Squad. Tell me, who was in charge? Who was the superior to these women who were under work obligation and who were otherwise employed in the iron ore mine complex?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Dusko who was the manager. I can't remember his surname. After all, this was in 1992. We know him as Dusko. And the manager of the whole complex, who supervised things so that there should be no breakdowns, was somebody called Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the immediate superior of the women was Dusko.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he kept a logbook of the working hours, and they received a personal income from the mine itself. Only later did they receive some addition from the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was Dusko's superior?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the butcher and the cook, who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: To me, or rather, we acted as a team who would meet in the morning. It was a meeting or a briefing at which we would agree on our activities for that day. Then we would make our own schedules or, rather, determine the food supplies, in what quantities, who would get them and prepare them for the main cook finally to be able to review the food and start cooking it. And of course, the butcher prepared the meat because he had to deal with large quantities of meat that were in the freezer and that were prepared for that particular meal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, who was in charge of seeing that the Quartermaster section should be supplied with the necessary foodstuffs with which to prepare the meals which you prepared?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: According to military structure and the chain of command, it was the assistant commander for logistical affairs whose job it was to ensure the necessary food supplies required for one day or, rather, three meals that were on the menu for that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the food was obtain, that is to say, where there was a sort of foodstuffs basis from which you received the food to prepare?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The -- it wasn't food, it was foodstuffs, foodstuffs to be cooked and prepared into a meal. And the procurement of this was from the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks from which we received our supplies which came to the kitchen in the iron ore mine where we were working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the kitchen located where you did your work? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The kitchen was located at the entrance on the left-hand side, as I -- on the first time, on the 22nd or the 25th of May, I entered that kitchen. I'd never been to the kitchen before that, and as I say, that was where the kitchen was located on one side. On the other side there was some kind of laboratory. So the first time I entered the cook -- the kitchen was on the 22nd or the 25th of May, 1992. That was the first time I entered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those buildings, that is to say, the building you prepared the food in, did it have a name of some kind? Did the people refer to it by some name that was customary?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: It was the administrative building. There were offices on the floor above, down below was the kitchen. I don't really know what the building was called. They were -- it was an office building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the building within the Omarska mine compound, or was it at some distance of the compound?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: It was where the Separacija building was where the iron ore was separated, and then down below that there were the dumpers, and that was 2 kilometres away from the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible from the Separacija building where you prepared the food to see the Omarska mine compound outbuildings?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, because it is at some distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What utensils did you have to prepare the food with? Did you have a military kitchen and all the utensils, or was it from the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The kitchen itself was equipped with all the necessary equipment and utensils necessary for the preparation of food. There were two big steam caldrons. There was a machine for peeling potatoes. There were two separate washing up basins for washing up, the heavy duty washing and the lighter washing. There was a special section for bread, another section for the foodstuffs, a separate storage space for the vegetables, and a refrigerator for meat, a freezer for meat. So it was a very up-to-date high-tech kitchen. A modern kitchen, I could say that, yes, a modern kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the kitchen belonged to the mine, did it? It was a built-in kitchen?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was owned by the mine, and the mine used the kitchen to provide hot meals for the workers working in the mine complex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the electrical energy, the electricity needed for the kitchen to function?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, we had electricity. That was our main source of energy. And later on I can tell you, or perhaps I can tell you now, that the situation was rather a difficult one because we didn't always have the necessary electricity which created problems for us when cooking the food or preparing the vegetables or heating up the precooked meals which had to be cooked slightly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any other source of power in case there was a power cut?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a generator which could be used in the kitchen, but the fuel was the problem with the generator, so that what happened sometimes was that a half-cooked meal had to wait for two more hours for the electricity to come back or for us to get the necessary fuel to switch the generator on for the meal to be fully prepared and cooked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, this system of cooking, what about the water supply necessary for the cooking, for the preparation of meals? How was that organised? Did you have a water supply?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Water came to us from a well. When the pump broke down, they intervened in Rosici and we were supplied with just one type of water which we used as drinking water, water for washing, and water for preparing the cooked meals. There were just one or two taps from which we could get water for our cooking caldrons - there were no other systems or other water supply at that time - and that's what they used to use before I arrived. The mine complex cooked the meals using that same water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, can I put it this way: Your work technology did not change, if I can use that term, compared to the cooking technology used beforehand while the mine was still functioning; is that true? You used the same cooking methods?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had the same potato peeling equipment. We cut the bread in the same way; we had the machine or we cut it by hand. We had the caldrons and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We've already heard about that. What was the capacity of the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, I consulted Dusko, but they were able to turn out between 800 to 1.500 meals for the workers working in three shifts in the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, where did the bread come from?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: We received the bread from the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks, and in the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks, they had installed field bakeries which worked for -- exclusively for the purposes of the army. They made bread exclusively for the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, you said that you prepared food for the members of the army. Did you or, rather, the sector you worked in with the women, prepare food in the course of June, July, and August of 1992 for somebody else, for other people?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 28th of May, I came to work as usual, at about 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning, and the main cook, Milan, told me that breakfast had been sent off for the army but that we had 2 kilometres away from us, a group of people who had arrived during the night and to whom a meal was distributed, a ration was distributed, cold ration. And he said that, "The assistant logistics commander ordered me to hand out food to those people, and I personally handed these tins and bread out to those people." Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be sufficient. Mr. Rendic, give us an example of how you prepared lunch, for example, but briefly. We haven't got much time.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: We would prepare lunch in the following way: As there were many meals to prepare, we started cooking lunch at about 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. in order to be able to turn out the necessary number of cooked meals that we were preparing. And lunch would be served between 8.00 and 9.00 for the camp. The second part would go to the army, to be dispatched to the army at about 11.00, which means that we would prepare the same meal, the same type of food, for both because we were not able, technologically speaking or with the capacities we had at our disposal, to make different meals, a variety of meals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, it means that your department, during the period that we're discussing, always prepared one meal of the same type, the same meal for members of the army and for the detainees in the Omarska camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, can you tell us -- give us an example of what one meal or one lunch consisted of.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I said there were two steamed cauldrons in which the meals were prepared, and in the first ten days we had sufficient supplies of all the foodstuffs. And when I say "foodstuffs" and "ingredients," I mean, for example, the basic foodstuffs necessary, and it usually was a potato stew. There were enough potatoes, there were enough vegetables, there were enough vegetable oils and fats to cook the -- and spices to cook the meal with. So for the first ten days, the meals were very good quality-wise and quantity-wise and was on a par with the standards provided for by the army. There was sufficient quantities. We had enough food and good quality food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us an example of lunch. Tell us the different types of lunches you prepared.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Usually there was bean stew, potato stew, peas. We used to combine having a heavier meal for lunchtime and a lighter meal for the evening meal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the first ten days? Was the quality of the food the same? Did it remain the same or what happened?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: After ten days, it became more difficult to come by supplies, to procure supplies. Krajina was cut off, as you know, not only with respect to food but with respect to other necessary materials such as sanitary material and so on and so forth. So there was a drop in the supplies which add taste to the food and lend it more caloric value. That is to say there was a shortage of fats and spices. Later on, the wartime food reserves that we were given, the food was not of such good quality later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you began to have supply difficulties, did the food continue to be the same for members of the army and for the detainees in the Omarska camp? I'm talking about lunch.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything was the same. We cooked the same meal which was dispatched to both groups, and the assistant logistics commander received complaints from the army members. They said, "How can the food have been so good for the first five days and not so good now?" So he had to explain to the soldiers that there was a shortage of spices to make the food tastier. So he said that there was a shortage of flour, of fats, and spices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, you and the people working with you that you told us about, that you enumerated, how long did it take you to prepare the meals and how many meals did you prepare in the Separacija building?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: We prepared approximately 6.000 meals. When I say 6.000, let me say that there were about 1.000 to 1.200 soldiers that we had to feed, which meant 1.000 breakfasts for the army, 1.000 lunches for the army, 1.000 dinners for the army, which makes 3.000, and the rest of the meals went to that unfortunate camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, can you tell us in numbers how many meals in the course of one day were dispatched to Omarska? I'm not talking about breakfast, lunch, and dinner, but a meal as one unit.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: You mean for the mine?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The first food supply prepared from 3.00 in the morning to 4.00 in the morning would be cooked by 8.00, 8.00 a.m. The food was then prepared and loaded into -- put into thermoses, big ones, and was dispatched to the camp while there was enough food. Then we continued to cook that same meal for the army from orders from the logistics commander. But we always cooked more food than we needed so that if there was any food left over, we would send the food on. So the thermoses were the same for the army and detainees. These were washed, sterilised, and so on. And when the meals were distributed - and this would take one or two hours - the thermoses would be returned with any leftovers, and once we washed these thermoses, we sent some more food down there. So there was not just one -- food was not only dispatched once, it was dispatched several times for as many meals as were needed. So actually, the kitchens worked round the clock, 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, you mentioned the transport of food both to the units and to the camp. Was your department in charge of transporting and distributing the food? If not, who was in charge of this?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: My section, because it was small and you can see the enormous amount of meals that we had to prepare, it was our duty only to pack the food and the bread, to put the food in these large thermos containers and to cut the bread up and put it in plastic containers, and the food was then taken over by two drivers and two soldiers who knew where they were to transport the food on to further, whether the food was being taken to the mine or to the army lines. Let me just add that from time to time, a TAM truck would be used as an auxiliary to dispatch this second round of meals if the other vehicle was not available. So we had two, the main vehicle and this TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, the soldiers or, rather, the individuals who distributed the food, were they members of the units you yourself belonged to but not your sector; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. They were quite different soldiers. These were soldiers whose sole task it was to dispatch the food as ordered by the assistant logistics commander. So I was not able to spare any men, actually. I only worked with women, so they weren't able to do that job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were members of the Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, soldiers from the TO. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the soldiers had breakfast, lunch, and dinner. What about the detainees, did they receive breakfast? Was breakfast, lunch, and dinner sent to them?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said the detainees, not the inhabitants, the detainees.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, the detainees were not sent breakfast, lunch, and dinner. I've already said at 8 a.m., 8.00 in the morning, was the meal. Perhaps it was beans, then we would send beans. If it was peas for that day, then we would send off the peas or the rice. So it was one type of food, one particular menu, and that menu would be dispatched to the detainees. It was one meal, one dish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did they receive one dish, Mr. Rendic?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that because, you see, from me to the distribution of food to them was a distance, so I don't know whether they had one, two, or more meals a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, let us try and clear this matter up again. Was it the same dish, let's say beans one day or peas another?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same dish served to the army. If it was potato stew one day, it would be a beef stew another day, and this was sent to the detainees as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the food you prepared for the breakfast for the army, was this sent to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the dinner?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, if they needed more food, because they were precooked dishes. But breakfast was tea and bread and butter or some spread, jam or whatever. That was breakfast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about bread, how much bread was distributed to the army and to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The standard for one soldier was 150 grams of bread. We had loaves of 600 grams, so this would mean a quarter of a loaf per soldier. But there were days when the situation was more difficult and when we were not able to meet that norm because there was not enough flour, there was not enough yeast, so I would receive less quantities of bread. And the quantity of bread I received, the amount of loaves I would receive, would be divided up into the meals so that there were days when recruits and the people who were in the camp as well would receive less bread than the prescribed norm. They would receive, say, an eighth of a loaf of bread. That was how we cut the loaf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, could you tell us when this bread restriction started? When was this period when there was a shortage of bread?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: It was a long period. When I say long, even one day was a long period, but this lasted for about 10 to 12 days. Right up until the time that fresh supplies of flour reached us. I don't know where the supplies came from. But private bakeries also helped us out and sent us some supplies, as the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks was not able to supply us with sufficient bread. The population had difficulty in coming by bread as well, not only us who were trying to meet the requirements of the army and, as I've already said, of the camp and its detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, you were a tradesman; you had a shop. Do you happen to remember -- can you remember how much a sack of flour in the Prijedor-Banja Luka area cost on the black market?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: It was very expensive. When you say expensive, it was expensive for us, and it was over 20 Deutschmarks, German marks, maybe even more, which means it was 100 per cent more expensive because we were cut off and, you know, supplies are used up very fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the situation the same with cooking oil and salt?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I've already said that we had a problem with fats. As I say, fats give a meal high caloric value, and there was a shortage of cooking oil and salt, spices. Detergent as well for washing. That shortage was felt previously because there was terrible rampant inflation so that the shops were empty. There were long lines for detergent, for example, and it was very difficult to come by those basics, basic food supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, did you ever go to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't able to because of all the work I had to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the work of your Quartermaster section? Did anybody of the civilian authorities control it? Was it under anybody's control?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who came to control you?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for logistics, Mr. Andzic, came to inspect us. Then there was Mr. Drljaca. I don't know what his function was, but I heard later that he was commander of the Crisis Staff of the CSB of Prijedor. So they would call upon me and ask me what problems I was having with respect to supplies and foodstuffs and the cooking of hot meals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Drljaca of the problems you were encountering? Did you inform him of the situation?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I said that all the reserves that the mine had, all the mine's reserves of salt, spices, cooking oil, had been used up, and what we were receiving were minimum quantities and that it was difficult for us to meet our assignment, to cook the meals with these shortages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he answer?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: He said, "Well it's wartime. What you have, you must prepare and distribute that food." I said that the army was boycotting the food we were sending out, that the army was -- the soldiers were refusing to eat the kind of food we were dishing out, and that was a problem that he had to confront. And he was an eyewitness. He saw this when he went to the front, he saw this happening, soldiers throwing the food away. And he was very angry with me, but I said we couldn't cook if we didn't have what to cook the meals with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of the work you did with these women, were you also in charge of preparing meals for the investigators?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We prepared food for them, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many meals?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Two meals, one between 10 and 11, and the second meal when they got home between six and seven, sometimes later, sometimes earlier, but they had two meals a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were their meals different? Were the dishes different, better quality compared to the food received by the army and the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: We would prepare their meals separately. They would have meat and salad, but they would have the same additions of vegetables, potatoes, and beans which were served to them as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Members of the Omarska police who provided security to the camp, did you also prepare food for them?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We also prepared food for them. They ate the same kind of food as the soldiers, except for the fact that the third shift, as they called it, had a kind of lunch package which included a sandwich.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the members of the security personnel, if they worked a 12-hour shift, they only had that one meal which consisted of a sandwich; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the kind of shifts they worked in. All I know was that they were sent some food, that is, the lunch package which consisted of a sandwich, between 6.00 and 8.00 or 10.00 because they were working this third shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the night-time?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is 2200 hours?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rendic, could any policeman from the Omarska camp have any kind of influence on your section in terms of improving the quality of food?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. Why? Because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is quite enough, Mr. Rendic. Thank you. Did any members of the security personnel of the police station have any ability to influence the quality of the food so that the quality of the food would be improved?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. They had a person who was in charge of procuring the supplies necessary for preparation for the food, and that person was the assistant commander for the logistics and the main base. That was the person who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, during the time that you spent working in the kitchen, did any member of the police station in Omarska ever pay you a visit during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, never. The doors of our kitchen were closed. We didn't have much time for socialising with people. We didn't have enough time to talk with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You live and you work in the centre of Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is that from the police department, from the Omarska Police Department?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Eight hundred metres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet the person by the name of Miroslav Kvocka in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his family?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Kvocka by profession?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman. As far as I know, he used to carry out patrols with Ljuban. So I would see him from time to time in the street. I was one of those residents who never asked any assistance from the police. I was a law-abiding citizen, so I didn't know him very well. I knew members of the police insofar as they were customers in my shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the father of Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew his father. I socialised with him, because for a period of time I used to travel to Prijedor where I was the manager of a restaurant. So I used to go to work at 5.00 in the morning, and the late father of Mr. Kvocka was a baker in the Zitopromet company. He was a poor man, a hard-working man, and I knew him very well. He had a lot of difficulties in his life. He died some time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, during the time when this Omarska camp was functioning, did the family of Mr. Kvocka have any threats from extremists in Omarska? Were they threatened in any way?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Omarska is a very small town, you know, and in the year of 1992, when people came from the front in Slavonia, when a lot of people were being killed, Mr. Kvocka, according to the stories that I heard, kept four or five members of a different ethnic community in his house, and I know that he was exposed to a number of threats by other people. They threatened him with blowing his house up. They called him a Serb traitor. But those were stories. I didn't have anything to do with that. And the times were very difficult, and only later on when certain units were established and where people went to war did the situation change, but those times were very difficult and a word could cost you your life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you knew Mr. Miroslav Kvocka as a policeman. Was he a problematic person? Was he a difficult personality? What kind of respect did he enjoy amongst his fellow townsmen?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew him. I know he was a well-respected man, that he was a professional policeman, and I know that he did not have any conflicts with the residents until the breakout of the conflict. He was a reliable person, the person one could work with, one could count on. He had a good reputation. He was well-respected in the town. He was a hard-working man and he lived his own work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rendic. I don't have any further questions for you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do Their Honours have any questions for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Rendic. We will see. Do other Defence counsel have any questions for the witness? No. Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Rendic, you will now be asked questions by the Prosecutor, and then after that perhaps the Judges will also have certain questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well did you know Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I knew him because he was a customer in my shop. I also knew him because I would see him from time to time in the street because I also moved around a lot, and I knew where his house was, and I knew his father's family, and I also knew his father personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you spoken to him? Did you socialise with him for you to give us such a recommendation?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Occasionally, yes. We may have gone out for a drink from time to time, and we would also talk to each other in my shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know as to where Mr. Kvocka was during 1992, in the month of May?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. All I knew was that he was at the police station, but I didn't know anything about his function there because I was very busy with my own work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the camp, in the Omarska camp? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him there. I never went there. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The witness answered the question, but he had also said previously that he had never been to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic, but the witness has already answered the question. If I am correct in reading the transcript, the witness said that he had never gone there. Yes. Mr. Waidyaratne, the witness has already answered your question. He said he had never gone to the camp. So if he had never gone to the camp, he could not have seen him there. So would you please strike your question or proceed with another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rendic, where did you work when you prepared this food? Where was this location or the building called the Separacija?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The building called Separacija was located at the entrance, at the main gate to the mine company. It was on the left-hand side where the kitchen was, together with the administration building, which included also a laboratory and the kitchen as well. I went there for the first time when I was assigned to do that kind of work, to organise the work that I was given as an assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rendic, to make it clear, to get to Separacija, the building where you worked, you had to pass the main gate in the camp. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. There was a junction, you see. Then there was the main gate, and on the left-hand side there was the entrance to the kitchen, that is, to the premises of the mine company, and the camp itself was 2 kilometres away from that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For you to enter this location, Separacija, were you showed with a special pass by the Omarska police?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, because everybody knew me. Of course, the guards who were manning the gate knew what my assignments in the mine company were. So the only document I had and that I needed was my military identity card which enabled me to enter the premises and to carry out my duties. The same applied to the people who were involved in the preparation of the food together with me. But there is another thing I would like to mention. Usually members of the Quartermaster's section know each other and they are very well known to other people. At that time, you know, there was a very big shortage of food and people knew us. They knew who we were and what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rendic, you spoke about a gate and the guards. At which place? What is this gate and the guards that you speak of?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: There was the main gate to the mine company, that is, to the administration premises which include the kitchen. There was the gate number 1. I don't know what it was called. I wasn't interested in that. Those were the guards in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of these --

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, the guards in the mine company. There was a man there who was from Lamovita. I knew him from sight. I knew that he was from the Lamovita village. There was another resident of that place which was called Obrad, and all those people knew me because I had a shop there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These guards, were they armed? Did they carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. At least I didn't notice that. I'm sorry I'm speaking too fast. I didn't notice that, and they didn't carry their arms -- they didn't carry arms when I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you said that you went to the Separacija building on the 22nd or the 25th of May, 1992. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Thereabouts. Yes. Yes, you're right, but I cannot tell you the exact date. It must have been around the 22nd of May that I was assigned to carry out the job that I have already described here, that is, to work on the preparation of food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told by -- whom did you -- who asked you to go to this place?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I have already said that the assistant commander for the logistics, Mr. Andzic, my superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went there, between this time, on the 22nd or the 25th of May, who was there? Whom did you take in charge? What did you take in charge?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I found between 12 and 15 cooks there, the women, who were preparing food for the employees of the mine company; and I also found Mr. Dusko, who was a manager there. Later on I was also introduced to Mr. Babic who was the administrator. And my task was to organise the work on the preparation of the food, and Mr. Dusko -- is that enough?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine. Now, during that time, there were no detainees in the camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went there to prepare for the people who were to come there; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: For the soldiers. No, no, no, no. No, nobody knew anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I will strike my objection because the witness has already answered the question, but the question itself was leading.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I arrived on the 22nd - I will respond to the Prosecutor - or on the 25th, I don't know, and of course I was in charge of preparing the food for the soldiers. So as regards Omarska where there were between 1.000, 1.200 people, those were the beginnings of my work. And this is what I told Mr. Simic: On the 28th when I came to work, the main cook told me that a group of people had arrived and that they had been given sandwiches, some dry rations, sir. So I believe that I was perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You are. So the first batch of detainees, according to your knowledge, arrived on the 28th of May; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the 25th to the 28th, how many meals did you prepare for the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I have already said that, between 800 and 1.200 meals depending on the kind of numbers I was provided with. The assistant commander for logistics was in charge of telling me how many meals were necessary for that particular day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that during the time that you spent in preparing the food, making arrangements, that you all had morning meetings or briefings. Who and who discussed? Who and who attended the meetings?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: As I said, there were only three of us men and that the rest of the personnel were women, and the assignments were given on an individual basis. There were people who were in charge of washing the dishes, of cutting vegetables, and we all knew what the main cook was in charge of. He would receive the necessary foodstuffs which were supposed to be cooked, and that was the part of work that he was responsible for. And he was also responsible for that part of the distribution, but he didn't know who the food was sent to. We had pots of 25 to 30 litres' capacity, and he would fill them to their full capacity, and then they would be sent off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, I apologise if I have to, you know, clarify certain positions, but you must bear with me, but in brief you can answer. I can't restrict you, but if it's possible if you answer in brief it would be very helpful. Try to understand the question that I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it is my nature. I always -- I'm always willing to provide explanations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, when the amount of people or the meals that you have to provide increased, who provided you with that number?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't ensure that. I only got commissions, and the assistant commander from the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks was the one who was in charge of transporting the food to the place where it was distributed. I did not take any part in that. I didn't know anything about the number of meals that had to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, I don't think you understood the question. Now, at the beginning you provided 1.200, as an example. Did it gradually increase? If it increased, how did you get to know about that?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Of course I knew it because of the quantity of foodstuffs that I would receive, because one day I had, for example, one loaf of bread, the next day I would receive ten loaves of bread, so it means that the number of people who needed it had changed in the meantime. It was logical. I just noticed at one point in time that the number -- that the numbers have increased. I realise that there were more beneficiaries than before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rendic, you said one time, in fact you told Mr. Drljaca that you needed more food and the quality of the food. Now, were you in a position to make requests for food, for provisions?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. I was only in a position to draw their attention to all problems and difficulties linked to the quality of the food. I was not able at any point in time to order larger quantities of food to be sent to us. As I told you, Mr. Drljaca said during a meeting that the situation was difficult and that it could not be improved, that people had difficulties in general, the population in general, but that referred to the soldiers and to the army. I don't know anything about the rest of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were not -- you said at certain times there were difficulties, and in providing the bread that you had a problem. When there was a shortage, whom could you tell, and what action did you take if there was no sufficient bread available?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: See, I was commissioned a certain number of rations. If for 6.000 meals one needs 1.500 loaves of bread and I received only 1.000 loaves of bread, naturally I had to ask myself what happened to the rest of the bread. But I didn't have any direct influence. I couldn't order any larger quantity of bread. This was something that could have been done only by my superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're simply saying that if there was a shortage, you were unable to do anything; you didn't care?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I wasn't able to do anything, of course. It was not within the scope of my competencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rendic, you said very briefly about the preparation, that the kitchen was well equipped.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you hear me? Yes, the kitchen was well equipped; however, the capacity was 1.000 to 1.500 meals. That was the actual capacity of the kitchen. Is there anything else that you would like me to say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So you were not in a position or it was impossible to provide 6.000 people; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was impossible, but given superhuman efforts and the fact -- the way we worked in the kitchen 24-hour day or around the clock, we managed partially to accomplish that, too. When I say partially, we may have been able to achieve it 100 per cent if we had the energy required. To prepare food, you need to have energy sources. And also to prepare good quantity -- good quality food in sufficient quantities, you needed fats, spices, and other elements to provide the necessary calories and the necessary taste to food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rendic, you said you provided food to the Security Services, the group that was in the camp, the detainees, and the interrogators. First I will get to the interrogators. Did you any time see interrogators having the food that you provided, their consuming the food?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. I said that I never went to the camp. The first meal was served, then the second. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can answer in a very short form whether you know, whether you saw. I asked you a simple question, whether you saw or not. Do you know whether they consumed that or --

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: They ate the food. I said that we would prepare goulash for them, for instance, a stew, then schnitzels, and then the side dishes were the same as those given to the troops. If there was rice, they would get rice. I didn't see them where they were working down there, but when they came back at 1800 hours or between 1800 and 1900, sometimes 2000 hours when they had the second meal, then they ate that meal in the restaurant of the mine complex. The restaurant was separate from the kitchen in another room, in a large hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that they had the meal in the restaurant, as you had not been to the camp, you don't know as to whether in fact they had?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Food was sent to them down there. I don't know who served their food. I think it was an employee of the mine. But the second meal, they ate that meal in the restaurant next to the premises where we were preparing food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see this -- now, you say, "In the restaurant next to the premises where we were preparing the food." Did you see the interrogators coming to the restaurant? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, I was resting because my working day was from 4.00 a.m. until 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., and they always came after that. So I too had a family, and I needed some time to rest. I would organise Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 everything so that they would come and their meal would be served to them by the cook. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to be a little bit more clear. Now, you didn't see them coming to the restaurant next to the premises that you were cooking in?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The kitchen is to one side; the restaurant is the other. The separation was just the self-service line that people would form. That separated the kitchen from the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question. Was this restaurant that you're talking about in the premises where you prepared the food?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I said that at the beginning. Because next to the kitchen was a self-service restaurant. You'd pick up a tray and take your food. So it was a self-service system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to ask you this question. Now, there was another kitchen and a restaurant in the camp. Have you been to that restaurant in the administration building?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. No, no. I had nothing to do with that. I didn't have the time physically to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rendic, what you're trying to say is that there were interrogators who came to the place -- to the restaurant which was in the premises where you prepared the food?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure we understand one another. The first meal would be sent to them to their workplaces. Where that was, I don't know. The second meal that they took after they completed their duties, they ate it in a dining-room adjoining the room where we were preparing the food. Do you understand now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I very much understand. That's why I asked you a direct question. You could have easily answered that question yes or no. Did you know any of these interrogators?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. They were people from Banja Luka. And thank God I never had contact with any of those people, so I didn't know any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say thank God that you didn't have any contact with these people?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Because throughout my life and career, you know when you do something wrong, you have to go to an investigator or a judge. I never had anything to do with such people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you scared of them?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. Why? If I was scared, I wouldn't be here today. So I'm not a scared person. I've come to tell the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, did any of the people who were detained in the camp come to the kitchen to help?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: In the preparation of the food, nobody. I did notice some persons washing the windows on the administration building, and that was at another entrance and not the entrance to the kitchen. So nobody could take part in the preparation of the food who didn't have a health certificate, who wasn't healthy enough and allowed to work with food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you very briefly give the names of the people who were involved in the preparation of the food? The cooks, if I may be specific.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Let me see. I know that the main cook was Milan Predojevic. The main butcher was Drago Vuceta. As for the others, the people who had duties connected to the preparation of food, were workers of the iron ore mines Omarska, and they performed the duties of cook in peacetime in the mine, and they were under the work obligation to assist us in preparing the food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, now you said that you were provided water to do everything, for drinking and preparation. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. No, you're not correct. Nobody brought water to us. There was water running from a water pipe. That was the situation we found in the mine when we arrived. The same water that they had in peacetime, before the conflict broke out. So that same water was used to prepare the food for the workers of the iron ore complex. So there was no delivery of water from the outside with tanks, barrels, containers, or anything like that. The same water was used for the soldiers and for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's for preparation. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: For preparation and for cooking and for washing, for everything. The same water was supplied to us for everything. If we needed to wash the potatoes, we used the same water. If we needed to wash the beans, we used the same water. If we needed to cook beans, it would be cooked in a large cauldron with that same water. So the same water was used for all these purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, you don't know as to whether the soldiers brought water from outside to drink?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: That was impossible. I didn't have five taps. There was no need to bring water supplies. We had sufficient quantities of water. Now, whether the soldiers, depending on where they were, couldn't use that water or maybe they used water from wherever they were. Omarska does not have a water-supply system. It has wells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, getting back to the meal again, when you said, if I understood correctly, was that you prepared the food, and it was given to soldiers to be taken to the security personnel and the people in the camp. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. No. The food was prepared, if we're talking about the camp, for the camp between 3.00 a.m. until 7.00 a.m. So the first batch of food was prepared that was then sent on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I do not want you to repeat what you've already said. To make it simple, I will rephrase my question. After the food was given to the soldiers to be transported, you don't know as to whether it reached those people or not?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. That was not my responsibility. The assistant commander for logistics was responsible, and he knew exactly where the food was going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or what time it reached those people concerned? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: There were different times for the transport of food as we were short of fuel and we had only one, sometimes two vehicles to transport the cooked food. Is any additional explanation required? The time for breakfast for the troops, do you need the times? Do you need me to tell you the time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You do not know as to whether when the food reached the people in the camp, the detainees, was spoiled or not?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the commander for logistics gave me orders that the first batch of food, that is, between 8.00 and 9.00, needed to be distributed down there between 12.00 and 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Rendic. The question was whether you knew or not. The answer should be yes or no. Did you know or not?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Whether the food was spoiled or not? Is that the question I'm asked to answer? I didn't quite understand it then. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know whether the food was spoiled when it reached the people concerned, the people that were to consume that, the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I don't know the context within which you wish me to answer that question. It is simply not possible for the food to be spoiled within such a short span of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, you said that the food was prepared at 3.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, how much more time do you need to complete your cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: About 10 minutes or 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We've going to have a break then. We'll have half an hour break. I will ask the usher to accompany the witness out, please. Half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. You may be seated, Witness. Mr. Waidyaratne, ten more minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, being the person in charge, the logistics person in the kitchen, did you keep any records of what was provided to you about the supplies?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't keep a record of supplies, but the supplies arrived, and whatever arrived that day was cooked for the next day, and everything had to be used up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make it clear, what you are trying to say is it was -- was it provided on a daily basis? Were the provisions sent to you on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were in the Omarska, this kitchen that you were referring to, did you see in the month starting at the end of May, the month of June, July, a busload of people being brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything because in view of the position of the kitchen, it was not possible for me to see that. The kitchen faced towards the east, and the road is to the west in relation to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rendic, you had been in the military services, and did it interest you or -- what was your understanding as to why all these people were brought to the camp? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I'll answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The witness was head of the kitchen. He doesn't know the type of prisoners; he didn't see them. How can he explain why they were brought there, and I really don't understand the purpose of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, what is the aim of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to whether he was aware as to why these people were brought. If he's not, he could say so, but being in -- working there for two months, providing meals for these people for two months, as to whether he was aware as to why these people were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question, please, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will make it more ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, what was your understanding or did you get to know as to why these people, the detainees, were brought to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I was not given any explanation. I just received the order to prepare the food, or rather, the cooked meal. I know nothing about who those men were, why they were brought there, who they are, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not made aware, but did you find out, being there for two months? Did you make an attempt?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. And of course, I learned from Mr. Drljaca the kind of people involved and who -- not really who they were, but what it was about. To be specific, I didn't know the aim, why they were brought there, nor the methods used. I knew that they were people from our area of a different ethnic group, but I don't know why they were brought there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I said Bosniak or Muslim ethnicity they were. Those people, why they were brought there, I told you I don't know why they were brought there, nor by what means I also don't know. I told you what I was doing there. My duty was simply to organise the work involved in preparing cooked meals for the troops and for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to go right back to the place where you started. When you came to the Omarska camp, were you in the 43rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. I was in the TO. I told you. I left the Motorised Brigade in 1985 or 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another matter. The last time I would go into this area. You said that you provided sometimes sandwiches for the shift which worked in the night, the third shift.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who requested you do that?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: At the request of the assistant commander for logistics or, rather, upon his orders, because they took over duty, and when dinner was being distributed, they were not there. They came to work at night, so we had to provide them a meal in the form of a lunch packet or a salami sandwich or a cheese sandwich, something like that. I'm sure you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, you said that two meals were provided to the detainees, one in the afternoon, which was a heavier meal, and one in the evening, a lighter meal. Was dinner provided to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. I said that one type of food was being prepared. So if it was, shall we say, beans for the soldiers for lunch, then before that, beans would be prepared for the camps. If for the soldiers rice was prepared for dinner and food was lacking down there, then any surplus would be sent there to make up for any lack of food down there. That's what I said at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So make it once clear. Only one meal was provided to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now about Mr. Kvocka. Did you know Mr. Kvocka's father?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him in person. We would travel together on the way to work. I was working in Prijedor. I was manager of a restaurant. He was working in the Zitopromet company as a baker, and we took the same train going to work and coming back from work. Not every day, perhaps, but we would meet often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in May 1992, during the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that. You see, I didn't have much time in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know as to when he passed away?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. When he passed away, it was a poor family. I know that they took some supplies from the shop, that they were in a very difficult position as a family. They were not well off, and knowing his sons, we assisted them to provide what is necessary for a funeral, which in our custom costs quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you. The question was whether you knew when he died. Just tell us the date. You don't have to tell us the whole story. Just answer the question when he died.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date when he died, but I know the financial situation they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Krstan Simic, your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I only have a couple of questions. Re-examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, when you were talking about the entrance to the mine complex at the gate next to the Separacija building, you said that there were guards there. Can you tell us whether they were military guards, police guards, or the security workers of the Omarska mine?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: They were workers in the security of the Omarska mine. I didn't see any other security officers. There was another gate also that I used to jump over sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the distance between the Separacija building and the camp is about 2 kilometres. How long would it take a vehicle to cover this distance from the Separacija to the mine complex where the hangars and the other buildings were?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, probably about ten minutes. It's an asphalt road. There are no major bends in the road, only one or two, so about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
