utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, let us make things a little clearer, although we've already discussed this. Once the food was packed, who took over the food to transport it to the soldiers, to the camp, and who brought back the containers after the food had been distributed?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: As far as the transport of food to the camp is concerned, there was a Zastava vehicle taken for that purpose. Two drivers were assigned by the assistant for logistics. Those two soldiers had the assignment, once the food was prepared, to load the thermos containers and the bread and drive that food to the place of distribution. As for the soldiers, the same vehicle would transport the food and distribute it among the units, depending on the number of soldiers deployed in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid my question was not completely recorded in the transcript. You said that the transport was done by a Zastava vehicle that was owned by the agricultural cooperative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it requisitioned for the means of that unit?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me also add, if that vehicle was late, then we would take a vehicle from the mine, upon approval from Mr. Babic who allowed us to use it to be able to transport the food for other units because of the delay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to these soldiers. Were they members of the Territorial Defence unit and under the responsibility of Mr. Andzic?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers were also from the Territorial Defence, but not of the kind of speciality that I had in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether they were members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the food was delivered, did those same men come back with the containers in which the food had been transported?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Everything had to be brought back for us to be able to use them again the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they the same men?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all members -- were they also members of the same military unit?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, members of the police station department had no contact whatsoever with the transport of food to the place of delivery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, do you realise how you worded your question? But let us hear Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Not only that -- I'm sorry. Your Honour, not only that it was a leading question, Mr. Simic in fact gave the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rephrase your question, Mr. Krstan Simic. Put your question but not in a leading way. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do so. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the policemen from the police station department have any contact with the transport of food to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. From the moment the food was taken over and loaded until it was transported, they had no contact with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, you're an experienced caterer. The containers in which the food was transported, were they special containers; if so, what makes them special?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. In the mine we found these thermos containers which were used by cooks to deliver food to workers working in various locations. These thermos containers keep the food warm. They're used specially for the transport of food. The same applies to military thermos containers that are used in the army to keep the food warm and preserve all its properties, but this food can be kept in these containers five to six hours on the outside. If it is very hot, then the food can go bad, but in the winter months, then the food can be kept in those containers for longer periods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, when we were talking about the price of flour, you said that a sack of flour cost 20 Deutschmarks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Everything was sold on the black market in those days. There was no normal sales. Everything was out of control in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but tell us, you said that in those days this was a lot of money. What kind of salaries were people getting in those days?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, the inflation was soaring, so if you didn't spend your salary the moment you got it, the next day you couldn't buy two packets of cigarettes for that salary. Am I clear?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you buy ten sacks of flour with your salary, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much could you buy?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: If I went to a shop and if flour was available, you could buy a sack of flour, a small sack of detergent, a bit of sugar, and that's all if you spent it the moment you got it. The minimum quantity you needed to keep a family alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rendic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krstan Simic. Judge Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rendic. I'd like to have a few clarifications to put certain parts of your testimony together. You mentioned at the outset that you were using the same cooking methods which were used when the mine was still functioning, and it could produce something between 800 and 1500 meals. That's what I understood. Then you mentioned that you would usually give something between 800 and 1.200 meals to the soldiers before the detainees came, which means that the soldiers would take something like 1.200 meals. The detainees came. Were your cooking methods adequate to provide for all the detainees? Because the margin is very small. The margin would be 300 meals.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I should like to say good morning to the Judge, to Your Honour, first. Let me answer the question. First of all, I said the food was top quality when we had the necessary supplies, and I said at the outset that the staff I found working there was not able to cater to the needs of 1.000 to 1.500 meals, which means they needed assistance. Do I make myself clearer? None of us knew what was to happen later on. We didn't know that we were going to be faced with the situation as it arose later on, so that I wasn't able to plan ahead, to plan in advance. Does that answer your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, my question is very simple. Did you have the capacity to provide for the detainees when your maximum was 1.500, as you said, and already the soldiers would take 1.200? Before the detainees came, you said you made 1.200 meals. So the margin was very small. Was that enough for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, no, it wasn't enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, there was some kind of food you mentioned like goulash and schnitzel and so on. Of course, that was never sent to the camp. That would be eaten on the spot, as you said, in the dining-room adjoining the room where the food was prepared. So that was never sent to the camp.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Certain quantities of food were sent, of meat, I'm sorry, of meat were sent, but very small quantities which didn't satisfy -- which weren't enough for even a meal. Now, some would get a piece, others wouldn't, but the quantity of meat wasn't enough and wasn't up to standard, up to the norm, because the conditions were just not able to cater to the norm, and my superiors knew about this lack of meat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, what was the weather like at that period? Was hot or cold? The summers are usually hot, are they?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was hot. Temperatures were high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because you said the good could be kept warm. But was there enough refrigeration, if it is hot, to prevent it from getting spoilt? In your opinion as an expert.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: You couldn't put a hot cooked meal into a fridge. Once the hot food had been poured into these large thermoses, these 10 or 20 thermoses, the food would be poured into them and the food would be dispatched, transported, and during that short space of time, the food would be kept warm. You couldn't send hot food into a refrigerator because the temperature difference would be too great. So the food didn't get cold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In your professional opinion, when the food can wait from 3.00 in the morning to the evening, for instance, or afternoon, would it remain healthy to eat, the kind of food you sent?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: What I said was this: We started preparing the food at 3.00 a.m., which means that we got all the supplies and then we started peeling them, putting them into the cauldrons, and the food started being cooked at 7.00. So it took some time to prepare. Then the food was poured into the thermoses at about 8.00 and the food was transported. What happened to the food after 9.00, I don't know. But I know that from 1.00 p.m., 2.00 p.m., 3.00 p.m., the commander would ask us for additional thermos supplies full of food for that part of the terrain, for example, which means from 8.00 to 12.00, that was the time that the food was actually there, when it could go bad from 8.00 to 12.00, but it all depended on the conditions that prevailed, that is to say, what kind of plates and other utensils were used down there. I don't know the utensils they had for serving the food, for dishing it out from these large containers to actually dishing it out further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You just mentioned two things which I would like to get more straight. You said the detainees were not sent breakfast, lunch, and dinner. You mean the food was sent once and then they would do whatever they wanted with it? Is that what you meant? Because your affirmation was the detainees were not sent breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, no, they weren't sent breakfast. They were just sent one main meal, one main course, one main meal or dish. And you know what you get for breakfast. Breakfast is standard. But the other meals, it was a type of one standard main course meal for the day. Now, whether that was divided into two meals or whether it was served to them in one meal, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But at least breakfast was not there. That's what I understood anyhow.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned you knew the father of Mr. Kvocka. Were you a friend of the family or just you knew the father?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, I just knew the father. We would meet on the way to work, in the bus or in the train to and from work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Concerning the information you gave us that Mr. Kvocka would lodge some people of different ethnic communities in his house, did you know that as a friend or was it common knowledge in the place?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I heard that from the population, from the locals, from the local inhabitants. They talked about that. But as I say, I had very little time to leave my unfortunate kitchen. I had to work all the time. But sometimes when I would go to have a coffee in a cafe or go to a shop, it was sort of talked about, the fact that there were several families staying with the Kvocka family, and that was why people despised this, despised him for it. But I made no comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did they not say any more specific things, like for instance they were his in-laws, for instance, or they were specific people? It was just a common rumour without a very specific number or kind of people?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I didn't know who the people were, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then you said there were threats to blow his house. Was this also firsthand information --

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- or just rumour? What was that? Did you know the people who threatened that?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I didn't know the people, but that's what the comments bandied around were. I heard that people wanted to blow the house up. These were difficult times, you know. People came back from the Slovenian front in coffins, and Kvocka's father's house was on the way to the cemetery. And people were angry, of course, because if their children and sons had been killed in that unfortunate war of ours, and there was somebody harbouring people in his own house, people from a different ethnic group, a different nationality, then of course people resented this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said the house was on the way to the cemetery. To your knowledge, was it ever attacked or stoned or anything?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rendic.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Rendic, I believe you said that the first time you came to look at the kitchen where you would be working was somewhere around May 22nd or May 25th and that people were preparing meals for the mine employees, the people who were there, and you realised there wouldn't be enough for you. Now, what happened after the detainees came to the camp? Did mine employees continue to be employed there? Did they get their food from your kitchen or someplace else? I mean, what happened to the food supply -- the food source for the mine employees, or did they just go away and not work there any more after the detainees began to come? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Can I answer? Well, it was like this: There was a part of the employees who used the food prepared for the army and for all of us. They, too, ate that food. They still kept on eating the food prepared by us. The employees went to work for the purposes of the army under the wartime conditions, and they, too, had their work assignment in the mine itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So that just to make sure I understand, when you were talking in your testimony about meals that would be prepared for somewhere between 1.000 to 1.200 soldiers, did that include the mine employees who were conscripted into the army, or was this part of the mine employees, extra, over and above, the 1.200 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that they were all the people who had been mobilised, the army, the population, the workers, the employees. So whether it was 20, 30, or 100 meals, it didn't matter. When you had such a large quantity, it didn't matter if you had this extra quantity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. My other question is, did you know at any time during the two months that you were working in the kitchen in the Separacija, did you know how many -- approximately around how many detainees there were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not know. My assistant commander knew that, and he said that about 3.000 meals should be sent to them down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So that source of information would allow you to guess or to think that there were maybe somewhere around the same number of people being detained as the extra number of meals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say to that. Our goal was 6.000 meals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: So for the army, 1.000, and more around here, that makes about 6.000, breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That would be 3.000. If it's 6.000 meals that were prepared every day, and you had around 1.000 or 1.200 soldiers times three meals, that's about somewhere around 3.000 which leaves 3.000 extra, right?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: And I said because the army received breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I understand from your testimony, but I simply want to verify it, that once the food left your kitchen in the thermoses to go to the detainees, you had no control over its distribution; is that right? In other words, you didn't have anything to do with the food when it got unloaded from the thermoses and distributed to the detainees; is that correct? So --

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you have any way to know in what quantities the detainees would get the food? You said they would get this same food that you would be sending out, at least one meal, same food as to the army. But did you have any idea what quantity of that food a detainee would get as opposed to, say, an army person who was getting the same food for one of his meals, or did you not know anything about what quantity of the food they got?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I knew nothing about the distribution of the food, quantity-wise or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned that you were 2 kilometres I think away from the camp, but you also -- so that you didn't see busloads of detainees coming, but you also mentioned that at one point you did see some detainees washing the windows around the neighbouring administration building, right? That's what my notes say, you did say that you saw some detainees doing some kind of washing of windows, something like that, maintenance work. Now, were there other occasions while were you in the kitchen where you saw any number of detainees, I mean, around doing some kind of maintenance work or anything else, or was that the only occasion that you ever saw, actually saw detainees during the two months that you were there?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: That was the only time. I saw a few women washing the glass, the windows. Who they were, I don't know, but I later learnt that they were people who were from down there, but who they were, I don't know. And that was the only time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And they were all or predominately women who were doing the washing of the windows?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: They were only women, just women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said you knew Mr. Kvocka, you knew his father well, and you knew him as a policeman who was patrolling the streets in Omarska. While you were working in the kitchen, did you know that Mr. Kvocka was an official of some kind in the camp? Did you know while you were in the kitchen -- you didn't know that he performed some functions over in the camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not know, and I didn't learn about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you learn about that at any point thereafter? If so, how soon thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I learnt about that only much later. When he came here. Before that, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, we heard from you that you learned, presumably from your own superiors or somebody, that at certain points when you didn't have the right ingredients and there were shortages of oil or fats or spices, that the soldiers were complaining or rejecting the food that was sent to them. But I think that you also told us that nobody from the camp ever came to visit your kitchen. Is that right? You said that other people from your crisis centre, Drljaca, and your own logistics centre would come and visit, maybe inspect your kitchen, but that no one from the administration, direct administration of the camp ever came; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: That's right. Nobody ever came from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If they didn't come, did you ever hear complaints from anybody working in the camp, from the officials, guards, or higher-ups, anybody working in the camp that the food was not good, not up to par?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about any complaints, but I did hear about complaints from soldiers who were mobilised at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But from nobody in the camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Were there times during the shortages that you talked about or even during the electricity problems you had, were there times when the quantity of the food that you were able to send over to the camp in the thermoses was considerably or markedly less than other times? In other words, the majority or all days, did the same quantity of the food go over to the camps or were there days when less quantity of the food went over because of the shortages that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: We didn't send less food. The only thing is that it wasn't such good quality food, and the food was late sometimes because of the electricity cuts, the lack of fuel. So we would be late in preparing the food. That's what would happen. And sometimes when we were cooking beans, for example, because the beans were from the war reserves and old beans and you have to soak them in the water the night before, and then if there was no electricity the next day, it would be half cooked and then you would need another one and a half hours to cook it with the generator going. So it was very difficult to cook the food, much more difficult than under normal conditions. So sometimes about 10 per cent of the overall mass of food, there were some beans that were not cooked well enough, properly, but you couldn't actually notice that. It was such a small quantity impaired to the bulk that when the food was sent out, you wouldn't be able to notice that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I only have two more questions. One would be, in your experience as a person who manages food and caters, if food that was healthy and fresh when you put it into the thermos containers and it was taken to another place and taken out of the thermos containers, say these bean soups or the goulash or whatever you were serving was taken out of the thermos containers and left sitting for four or five hours before being served to the people that ate it, would there be a problem of spoilage then?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Of course there would be spoilage. It depended on the receptacles that the food was put into, poured into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand. My last question. It concerns the water. You told us that you basically used the same water from the same wells and the same taps for food preparation, for drinking, for whatever you needed it for. Did you use the same taps all the time or the same well source or were there many different ones around the area and you used them indiscriminately or you used them all or did you use just one or two special taps, and were they close by the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: The taps -- each cauldron had a tap, and so the taps were where the plates were washed, where the pots and pans were washed, and where the vegetables were washed. It was the same water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Mr. Rendic, I myself have three questions to ask you, and the first is the following: You said that from time to time there was a lack of food in the camp. Is that right? Did I understand that correctly, not enough food?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, no, there were not enough foodstuffs that were supplied to us in the kitchen where we then went on to prepare and cook the food. And facts -- some ingredients were lacking, that is to say, cooking oil and salt and spices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you never learnt that there was a lack of food in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that you never had information about the lack of food in the camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No. No, I had no information of that kind at all, because there was a man in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. My second question is the following: The people transporting the food from your kitchen to the camp, were they the same people who brought back the empty containers? Is that right? They were the same people who brought back the empty containers?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were usually the same people. They transported the food down there and brought back the containers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What time did they come back with the empty containers, with the dishes? What time?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: As we used the same receptacles, the same containers for the army, and we sent out the food for the army at 12.00, which meant that the containers had to be there at 11.00 or 11.30 so that they could be washed and used again, to pour the food into them and take them up to the front line to the soldiers. So these same containers were used by them down there and the army. So it was a circle. It was a continuous circle because we didn't have enough of the these thermal containers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, for me to understand you better, what time did the food leave your kitchen for the camp?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: I said between 8.00 and 9.00. That was the first shipment. And I don't know when they distributed the food in the camp, but the empty thermos containers were returned to us, to the kitchen, between 11.00 and 11.30, where they were washed and filled again to be sent on to the army. The remaining thermoses down there were brought later on, if any remaining ones stayed on. But as I say, we had a shortage of everything, thermos containers and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These thermos containers, were they individual ones or were they larger ones?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Well, I have already said, Your Honour. I said at the beginning that they were 20-, 30-, 50-litre containers. I said that to begin with. And even smaller thermos containers would be for five, ten, 20 people. So those were the smaller ones. The other ones were the large ones, and that is what is referred to as thermoses in army terms. Now, the thermos containers that we found in the mines were larger, a little larger than the army thermos containers, and I found them in the kitchen. They had been used previously by the mine. I said all this to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And now my third question. We know that you like to give explanations, and, therefore, I would like you to explain one matter to me. I think I heard you say that you took the number of meals -- that you knew the number of meals by the amount of foodstuffs you came to prepare the meals with. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We would get the foodstuffs in the afternoon for the meals that were to be cooked the next day. Now, if we had 500 or 600 kilos of potatoes, I would have to peel those potatoes and we knew that that would be the number of meals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but why did you have to divide a loaf of bread into eight pieces so that every person receives an eighth of a loaf of bread?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: That wasn't what it was like at the beginning, to begin with. That was the situation later on with the short supply of flour and yeast and everything else you needed to make bread. So instead of receiving 1.000 to 1.500 loaves of bread, I would receive less, and then I would have to divide up all the bread, which meant that rations were reduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you received less quantity did that not mean for you that there were less people, or did it, less people to feed, or did it?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: No, the same number of people remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why then do you say that if you received a lot of foodstuffs, there are a lot of people to be fed; and that would mean that if you received less foodstuffs, there would be less people to feed? Do you follow my logic of my question?

utterances.speaker: PERO RENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question, but I had to divide up what I was given, what I received, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understand you, yes. Mr. Rendic, we have no further questions to ask you. You have come to the end of your testimony. We thank you for coming here to The Hague, and we wish you a good trip back to your place of residence, and every success in the work of your restaurant. I will now ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to thank all Your Honours. Thank you very much, and I wish you Judges all the best as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to the list, I would like to call witness Miro Bijelec at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bijelec. Can you hear me? You will first read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated now. Make yourself as comfortable as possible. First of all, you will be answering questions that Mr. Krstan Simic will put to you. Mr. Simic, your witness. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bijelec.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know, my name is Krstan Simic, and together with Branko Lukic, I represent Mr. Kvocka in this case. In that context, I will ask several questions of you relating to your life and work in the course of 1990. But let me first ask you to pause a little before you answer my questions so that the interpreters can interpret my question and your answer subsequently. May we begin?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, we may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, could you state your name please?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Miro Bijelec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Bijelec?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of June, 1943, in Arandzelovac in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live today?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka in Jevrejska Street, number 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: In Dzakovo in Croatia, and the last six months in Gorazde in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, what did you do in your life? What was your occupation? But try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I was a sportsman, and I also had a private catering business, a cafe which is called "988" in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of sports did you practice?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Handball.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you an active player?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, from 1958 until 1976.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what club did you play?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: In Borac which was a handball club in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it an important handball club?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: By all means. During -- in the former Yugoslavia, the club was the federal champion six times. It won the cup ten times, and it was the European champion once in 1976 [Realtime transcript read in error "1996"].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before becoming champion of Europe, did you play in any finals?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995 we played against the German club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the record so let me rephrase the question. When did the handball club Borac become the champion of Europe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The transcript read "1996." Did you have any other titles?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991 the club was also the European champion, but at that time I no longer played. I was a -- I was the club's manager at that time. I was on the managerial board of the club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, it seems that we are having problems with the speed with which you give your answers, so I should like to remind you once again to pause before answering my questions. Did your generation become European champions?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, but I played in two generations. On the first occasion it was in 1957 when we became members of the Yugoslav league. I was 19 years old -- I was 15 years old at the time, and I continued with the same generation which eventually became champions, and they achieved the best results in the history of the club, that is, they were the most successful club in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later on in Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, Borac, the handball club, did it have other players who played in the federal selection?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: They won 13 gold medals in the Olympic Games, and we won seven world championships and a number of gold and bronze medals. And recently the club won third place in the championship of -- in the European championship which took place in France yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, Abaz Arslnagic, did he ever play as a member of Borac?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. He played in the year of 1964 up until 1976.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim, that is, what we call today a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you closely related with that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. I was his best man, was his kum. Our families knew each other for a very long time. Minister Karalic, who was a member of the government of Mr. Dodik, is also kum of Mr. Golic. Then Momo Golic is kum to Dr. Nebojsa Popovic who now lives and works in Liege and who is a member of the managerial board of the standard football club from Liege and I'm also a kum to Abaz Arslnagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, once again. Mr. Bijelec, I have to remind you of the necessity to make pauses between questions and answers. Let us talk about this type of relationship, that of being a kum to someone. What does it mean in our parts of the world?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: To be a kum to someone means something more than being his friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it normal for kums to socialise, even after the ceremony has taken place?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Not only kums, but also their families and children. It is perfectly normal for them to socialise, to visit each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Arslnagic do when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: In the state of Quatar. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He was the coach of the local handball club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Arslnagic, was he at one point in time the coach of the Yugoslav selection in handball?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, but he was also the coach of the Croatian selection and also the coach at one point in time of the Borac handball club, and also the coach of the junior selection of Yugoslavia who won first place, the gold medal, during the world championship in 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- what is -- what are the relations between you and Mr. Arslnagic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: The very -- we're on very good terms, and more than that. I must add that the apartment which had been requisitioned during the war has in the meantime been returned to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Arslnagic returned to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, can he just spell the name of Mr. Arslnagic because we have difficult writing it.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: A-r-s-l-n-a-g-i-c [as interpreted]. Do you need his name as well? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your career as a sportsman, what did you do? Please pause a little.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I stayed at the club as the manager. I wanted to ensure that Borac continues with its successes and its results, which involved bringing in new players, new coaches, taking care of the players, and taking care of the overall conditions in which the club functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, do you really need all of the details involved in the glorious history of this handball club? Do we really need this? Please proceed, but I think we can speed up things a little bit. We are not here to judge about the glorious past of this club. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I am aware of that, Your Honours, but this was an introduction to the events connected with the handball club Borac, which was a prominent club and involved in the social and political life of the community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Communist League previously?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1990, when conditions were created for multi-party elections, were you involved in the work of any of the political parties which appeared in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that political party?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I was a member of Ante Markovic's party, which was an association of reformist forces, and at that time, Mr. Markovic was the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, were other political parties created in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. There were, first of all, national parties, and the creation was made possible by the constitutional changes. The first party to be established was HDZ, then SDA, and finally SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the leader of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: You mean in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: In Croatia, it was Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: It was a very good friend of mine, Stjepan Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know Mr. Stjepan Kljujic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Stjepan Kljujic was a journalist who covered sports events, and he used to travel with us a lot within Yugoslavia and abroad, and he was connected with my club Borac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the leader of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: At the time it was created, it was Dr. Raskovic. When he passed away, Dr. Karadzic became the leader in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he remained on that function until the very end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, what was the support that the nationalist parties received, I mean of the HDZ, SDA, and SDS, in 1990 in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: At the beginning, it was rather difficult. The people had certain misgivings about such parties. They did not trust them at the beginning. However, they were very active in their rallies at the beginning. They even held rallies together, saying that they did not have enough freedom, that they could not freely act. So the situation lasted -- such situation lasted for a certain period of time, but later on, each ethnic community joined their respective nationalist party more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in 1990 you also joined the Alliance of Reform Forces of Ante Markovic, the then Prime Minister. Did that political party start to build an infrastructure in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: At that time, there was a big change within my club. We knew - I mean we at the club - that nothing would happen with these nationalist parties. And when Ante Markovic appeared and when he announced that he was about to create his own party called the Alliance of Reform Forces, we gave him our support, and I personally declared publicly that the members of Borac would become members of his party because it was a reformist party, and we identified ourselves as members of this local sports club with the policy of the Reformist Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to your handball club. Did it consist of players of various nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. There was one Croat, there were several Muslims. Dobrivoj Selez was a Croat, Hasanovic was a Muslim, and so on and so forth. I can give you many examples of that. It was a multi-national club as opposed to the football club Borac which was mostly a Muslim club, and the basketball club Borac which was mainly a Serb club. We were the only club that was multi-national.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Ante Markovic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He was a Croat from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe he was born in Konjic. He was an electrical engineer, and he came to Zagreb to take up his duties as Prime Minister, but before that he was the manager of the Rade Koncar company which was based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the assignment that you were given when the branch of the Alliance of Reform Forces was created in your place?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: It was rather spontaneous. There was a meeting that was convened, but we talked freely during that meeting. There was not any particular agenda. There was a number of intellectuals there who attended the meeting, including Zivko Radisic, Ivo Tabakovic, who was a member of Ante Markovic's government. So we talked awhile during that meeting, and we agreed that we should establish -- we should create a kind of steering committee for the purposes of establishing a branch of this party. And on -- that was on the 11th of September, and on the 12th of September, the steering committee was established, and that's how it all began. Each of us given particular assignments, and we started actively working on our assignments until the 15th of September, when we went to Sarajevo to attend the conference, and that took place on the 15th of September, 1990, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the reformists were getting organised in Banja Luka. What was your specific task within that branch?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Well, my task was similar to the one I had within the club as to how to organise new members, how to work in the area of Banja Luka, how to function as fast as possible because other parties were far ahead from us, that is, the nationalist parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of this new organisation, did they go out into the field?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a number of meetings. First such meeting took place in Kotor Varos. Ranko Zrilic was there. He was the dean of the engineers' faculty in Banja Luka. Marijan Benes was there, who was a famous boxer from Banja Luka. Milorad Karalic also attended the meeting. He is the Sports Minister in Dodik's government. There was another sports journalist from Banja Luka. We all went to Kotor Varos, which is some 20 kilometres away from Banja Luka. There were a lot of activities taking place at that time, but I didn't have any prominent role in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the group of people who went to Kotor Varos. Let me repeat the names of the people that you mentioned. Mr. Marijan Benes, what was he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He was a Croat that came from Tuzla to Banja Luka some 30 years ago. Sorry, 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a public personality? Was he famous?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, he was, because of the results that he had achieved both in Yugoslavia and in Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what sport?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: In boxing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Abaz Arslanagic was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also a public figure?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was the best goalkeeper in one of the world championships in France.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his nationality?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also a public figure?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we didn't get the name of the last personality involved.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He was famous. He was the captain of our team when we were champions of Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we repeat this question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness slow down.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: We were talking about Milorad Karalic. He was a professor at the Faculty of Economics, and he won many medals as Arslanagic. He played 251 times for the former Yugoslavia national team, and by ethnicity he is a Serb. MR. K. SIMIC:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Tomo Maric.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He's half/half. His father's Serb, his mother a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, the other members of the reformist forces, could you name some of the most prominent figures in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: There was Emir Kusturica, a well-known film director in Yugoslavia and on a world scale. Then Goran Bregovic, the well-known leader of the Bijelo Dugme rock group, and then Dragan Kalinic who is President of the Assembly of Republika Srpska but at the time he was a member of the reformist forces. Ivo Tabakovic, a professor and doctor of chemistry. I think he's living in London now. Then there was Professor Nenad Kecmanovic, dean of the university in Sarajevo. A poet and screenplay writer, Abdulah Sidran from Sarajevo. Professor Dzemal Sokolovic, also a university professor in Sarajevo. So there were quite a number of these prominent people who were members of the reformist forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of Abdulah Sidran did not go down in the record.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim and a poet. Sidran. He wrote the screenplay for Emir Kusturica's films.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about Banja Luka, were there prominent figures in Banja Luka who were members of the reformist forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Brana Trivic, who in the previous system was President of the Socialist Alliance. She was a handball player also in the Borac club of Banja Luka. Then Dzevad Haznadar, a well-known businessman from Banja Luka. And at the meeting, Zivko Aleksic, now a member of the Presidency also attended. He was a president of the board of management of Borac for two mandates, but at the establishment meeting on the 12th in Banja Luka, he did not appear, and though we see each other on a daily basis, I still haven't asked him why he didn't come then. But later on, he joined the Socialist Party and headed it in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, in those days, that is, in 1990, did Mr. Markovic come and visit the area? Was there a meeting at which he spoke?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: He said that he would make an address on Mount Kozara on the day of the uprising of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 27th of July, that is, the day of uprising from the Second World War. And this meeting was scheduled in 1990, and roughly 20.000 to 30.000 people attended this rally. However, he did encounter some difficulties and problems caused by the nationalist parties, first of all, by the SDS, who said, "Now, why did he choose this particular place in Bosnia-Herzegovina?" that he was doing it on purpose to the Serbs. "Why hadn't he done it in Croatia?" And we already know that the HDZ had made a great deal of progress in its structuring in Croatia. And then the SDA also said that -- opposed it because they were for a unified Bosnia and succession from Yugoslavia. SDA was headed by Alija Izetbegovic. We knew of his Islamic declaration for which he was sentenced to 12 years of prison in the previous system and later released. So these were the various criticisms, and they all boiled down to an unwelcome, to a meeting -- a welcome that he was not -- not a proper welcome given to Ante Markovic when he arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina on Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, the Alliance of Reformist forces of Ante Markovic, was it a multi-ethnic party where ethnicity did not count?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the aims of this political party?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: The aims were to provide the best possible conditions of life in Yugoslavia, to keep Yugoslavia whole, to overcome hyper-inflation, to reform the economy. He established a convertible currency and progress was being made. And he had a familiar saying, "Everything that is not prohibited is permitted." And we took advantage of this in the Borac handball club. We started setting up our own firms to provide finances, and this was something that was not allowed in the former system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I omitted to ask you a moment ago when you made a statement as a public figure that Borac would join the reformist forces, what were the media reactions?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: They weren't very favourable. I did make a statement for a newspaper, Banja Luka Glas, and then the former director, Andjelko Kozomara, who was a journalist at the time in the TV and radio of Republika Srpska, he branded me a traitor, that I was a Croat, et cetera, various things like that, which I considered it normal. I had expected to be attacked. This didn't just apply to me, but everyone else. That was the kind of atmosphere that prevailed in Banja Luka in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally have any unpleasantness stemming from your co-citizens because you had opted for the reformist forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I had to send my son to Belgrade to school, then my -- there was threat that they would blow up my cafe. Then, what is a Croat doing at the head of a club? There were telephone calls and things like that, but I bore it all bravely. I have big shoulders, so I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, you had reports that other prominent members of reformist forces had unpleasantness.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, my kum, Arslanagic, they broke into his apartment. They stole his goods; then they moved people out. So there were incidents of that kind. Momo Golic, who is now the director of Borac, was threatened by phone. Why is he keeping Croats and Muslims there? Why doesn't he throw them all out? And things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelec, during the war, was the captain of Borac a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, Arnautovic. He won Olympic medals, gold medals, and a world champion. He is now in Belgrade coaching the women's team of the club Buducnost, I think. Arnautovic is his name, Arnautovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the captain of the Borac team during the war who was a Muslim, but letter by letter. Please spell it for us for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: A-r-n-a-u-t-o-v-i-c. First name is Zlatan, Z-l-a-t-a-n.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Ranko Timarac?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Of course I do. He used to be a waiter in my place. He worked for ten years. He comes from Omarska. After he went to work in the Cyrano restaurant, then he opened his own restaurant in Omarska. The other day he had a traffic accident. He's still fighting for his life. I know him well personally, and my son and his went to the secondary school of economics together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, excuse me. Perhaps now would be the time for a break. Would that be convenient, or are you about to complete your examination? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I need another five or six minutes but I don't mind. Either way, Your Honour. Whatever you decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're going to have a break, and we'll come back at 2.00. Mr. Usher, please accompany the witness out. We'll be back at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Bijelic, we're going to resume the proceedings. Mr. Krstan Simic, you said you needed another five or six minutes, and I now give you the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the meeting, Mr. Bijelic, you mentioned a man called Ranko Timarac. Did he contact you with respect to the setting up of the Reformist Alliance for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. He came with a policeman, and the name was Miroslav Kvocka. I remember the name because Kvocka, his surname, means an egg-bearing hen. So I remembered the name. And they asked how they could become members of the Reformist Alliance or, rather, how they could set up the party in Omarska. However, our rules provide for the fact that parties can be established in a municipality, which means in Prijedor, and this would give us an insight -- the necessary insight we need for the voting. So I gave them instructions as to how this is done. They left but returned several days later to say that things were very difficult there, that it was impossible to set up a party there because there was the SDS and SDA parties who had divided up the population. They were equally strong, more or less. I was not able to accept that, and we decided that they should be more aggressive in their approach to setting up this party, that they should try and find prominent figures, prominent public figures. I think they found Mr. Ljuban Andic from Omarska, who is a lawyer by profession and a respected one, and then there was Nedjo Delic, who was the owner/proprietor of a restaurant called Evropa, and that they should report back to me. They didn't contact me later. Timarac came on one occasion and he said that he wasn't able to establish a party over there, that things were difficult, and so that's what happened. And let me also add that Kvocka had said he had been working abroad, that he was a policeman, and that he had always been brought up by his family that he was a citizen of Europe and not to go to war and that his main objective was to be a member of that party so that he could influence the rest of his fellow citizens. And we asked -- they asked again to be admitted into the party in Banja Luka, but we weren't able to do that and that's how the whole episode ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelic, the elections took place on the 18th of November, 1990. Could you tell us who the winners -- who won the elections?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: There were nationalist parties, and 80 to 90 per cent of them -- got 80 to 90 per cent of the votes. Our party did not go through. There was the well-known drama that took place in Bosnia, and we know how that ended. So we did not succeed. We were not successful in our attempt to form -- to do what we wanted to do because the nationalistic parties had far more voters and like-minded people who were ordinary people. They weren't educated; many of them weren't literate. And so that's how things went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the elections which were held and the establishment of power and authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in its municipalities, was a chance given to the members of the reformist forces to become part of the authorities in any of the municipalities? Were they given that opportunity?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No. At least not in Banja Luka, as far as I know, and the other places either. They were not able to make up the establishment, so to speak. And our former premier, Mr. Dodik, led in that respect, but he wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelic, after the elections that took place on the 18th of November, 1990, which parties took over power and authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Could you name them?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: The SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. They were the nationalist parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Dodik who was until that time the premier of the Serbian government. Was he a reformist as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, for the Bosanska Krajina region, and I think it was most difficult for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness, but I should like now to stress that the Defence within the prescribed procedure has announced two affidavits which support the Bijelic testimony. They are the affidavits of Mr. Dejanovic, member of the SDS party, who spoke about the relationship of the SDS towards the Reformist Forces Alliance; and the second affidavit is the statement by former premier of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Milan Dodik, and his testimony is linked to the relationships among the nationalist parties and the Golgotha that the sympathisers of the Reformist Alliance of Ante Markovic had to go through. Furthermore, I should like at this point to tender an exhibit. It is a document entitled, "Criteria for the Distribution of Municipal Posts and Departments," established between the representatives of the national parties of the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. And this was Defence exhibit, according to our own registry, D96, and the registrar has the exhibit under D62/1. D62 -- I'm sorry, D42/1. This document was signed by the then leaders of the nationalist parties in Sarajevo on the 22nd of December, 1990, and they are Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, president of the SDA party; Mr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the SDS party; and the man mentioned, Stjepan Kljujic, the president of the HDZ party. I should now like to hand you all these documents, and let me say that in the process of disclosure we received the document where it was mentioned that no other party of a leftist orientation shall not be considered and cannot be considered. That is a note at the end of the document. So could I have these documents handed out, please, to the Trial Chamber and the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, you wish to have the document distributed? I think that we already took this subject into consideration, Mr. Simic. The document -- I am going to give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers in a moment, but let me make this observation before I do so. The document wasn't used during the testimony. What I can see is you mentioned the document as being in existence and your intention to have it tendered into evidence. We've already said that the documents that you do not in fact use during the testimony should all be submitted in bulk so that the Chamber and the Prosecutor can examine them and then decide whether to admit them or not. So I don't know why at this stage you are bringing it up. The witness did not mention the document, and you now want to have the documents tendered and admitted. But before I go any further, I'll give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not even clear of the relevance of the document. I have not seen the document, and it was not put to this witness. So in the -- given those three points, I would ask at this time that we have a chance to look at it. Certainly to simply shove a document in whose relevance may or may not be established would be a mistake, I think, and if we could look at it and perhaps at the end of our examination and let the Chamber know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, your response. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have understood your suggestion with regard to certain documents which we have sent out; however, most of the witnesses did not have occasion to see this document. But Mr. Bijelic testified here. He said that after the elections there was absolutely no possibility for the reformist forces or any other force, apart from these nationalistic - and I like to say nationalistic and not national parties - that these nationalistic parties divide up power amongst themselves. And we wanted to show you an authentic document, tender it, which is connected to the testimony made by Mr. Bijelic and confirms that the reformist forces were removed from the political scene in Bosnia-Herzegovina because of the victory of the other nationalistic parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. Those forces were rejected. We are now arguing and counter-arguing and presenting allegations. I have already said that you should submit the documents to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution, and we shall examine them and decide whether to admit them or not, Mr. Krstan Simic. Otherwise, we are going to enter into a process of allegation. When you say that you want to show that the reformist forces did not participate in the government, how does this tie in with the core of the process, the heart of the matter? We did indeed hear the witness testify at length, and I am looking at the summary of the witness's testimony, and it is within that framework that the first secretary of the reform party, that he met him and Kvocka. But what was the essential reason for that? If you could explain that to me, I shall perhaps be able to understand. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence wishes to show the attitude of the government and the institution towards individuals who supported the Reformist Party and who advocated these ideas. This is related to the indictment charging Mr. Kvocka, as something that is contrary to what the witness is saying and what this document is saying and to what Mr. Kvocka did. This document should be related to the testimony given by Mr. Bijelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then, Mr. Simic. As we have already decided, you will submit the document. The Chamber will consider the document, and we have already been advised of the relevance of the document, if I may put it that way. After the opposing party has expressed its view, we will take our stand. So we do not have to discuss the issue at this point. We will admit it. But I should like you to link up the documents with the matter that is being discussed. We are not going to discuss whether the document is going to be admitted or not at this point. It has been admitted, and we will see about it later on. You have finished with your examination-in-chief. Ms. Somers for the cross-examination or Mr. Saxon? Who is going to cross-examine the witness, please? Yes, but before we do that, I'm sorry, I have to ask whether any other Defence counsel have questions to ask of this witness. It seems that they do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may just take a quick look at this document, Your Honour, before I begin. Thank you. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelic, your very brief encounter with Mr. Kvocka took place exactly when, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: It took place in early September when we started establishing steering committees and taking new members to the party. The matter received a certain amount of publicity by Banja Luka papers, in particular because of the fact that people heard about our wish to do that. So Ranko Timarac, who worked for me at the time and who had an agreement with him at the time, he was supposed to organise a group of people in Omarska, a group of people that he knew, so that we could have as many members as possible. That was our objective at the time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 As regards the exact time, whether it was on the 12th, the 13th, or the 14th of September, I don't know, but it all took place between the 10th of September and the end of September, but I cannot be more specific than that in terms of date. But they came to see me on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the year, please? September of which year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Miroslav Kvocka wearing-- what was he wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember that. It was ten years ago. I really cannot remember how he was dressed at the time. I simply don't recall. He was wearing some kind of sports clothes. It was the beginning of fall. He wasn't wearing any coat or jacket. I remember that it was sunny. It was not cold. There was no snow. The whole thing took place in the Bosna Hotel. You know, we would meet between 30 and 40 people per day, and it's difficult for me to remember who wore what. And even if you asked me what I was wearing at the time, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I thank you for searching your memory. Can you tell us, please, was he coming to you in the capacity of a police officer or as a private individual?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: As a private individual. Ranko Timarac was the one who spoke more because he didn't know me. He said that he was a policeman, that he had worked abroad, that he was interested in helping us in establishing the branch of the party in the area of Prijedor, the SRS party. But we didn't know each other very well at the time. I just remember the name Kvocka because, in our language, it means "hen." So that's how I remembered his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the individual who was screening persons who wanted to start up perhaps new chapters or branches of the Reformist Party, as you're calling it? Were you the screener of this?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the only person who did that because I knew the area of Banja Luka very well. I knew what people did, and I was the only person who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. Kvocka why he became interested in your party?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Well, he said that he had worked abroad. He didn't tell me what exactly it was that he did. Then he said that he was brought up in a European spirit, if I can put it that way, and in the same spirit as I was brought up and Mr. Krstan Simic as well. He knew that nationalist parties were not good. He knew -- he understood what was happening. He probably analysed it, and he really wanted to be the most prominent person of that particular branch, and they were not able to do anything, neither him or Ranko Timarac, without proper support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to that conclusion after the brief encounter you had in which Mr. Timarac spoke on behalf of Mr. Kvocka? Did you conclude that based on that interview?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No. See, during that first encounter, I did not come to that conclusion because the situation was such that we had a lot of work to do. We had to establish the steering committee. So we were working very fast. On the second occasion when he came, we realised that he was really willing to become active, and we talked at a greater length. Kvocka wanted us to be more aggressive in our approach, but it was difficult to establish smaller branches or chapters without having a steering committee in Prijedor. We wanted to have a proper register so that we would know how many voters we could count on, how many members of our party would be amongst our voters because the objective, of course, for us, was to win the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on these two encounters, did it appear to you that Mr. Kvocka was a man who would undertake leadership responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was my opinion of him, and Ranko as well, because they were very persistent and they seemed to be knowledgeable about the situation. He knew many people there, and I thought that they would be successful in establishing that committee in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help us understand a little bit more about this institution called the Reformist Party. Was it in fact a party, or was it an alliance that was formed to unify certain parties? How would you best describe that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: It was a reformist party which was in favour of Yugoslavia, and it was our objective to have the state of Yugoslavia preserved. That was our objective. That was what we had in mind, because the situation was really good at the time Ante Markovic was the prime minister. He managed to control the inflation, we stood very good chances of joining the European Union, and it was perfectly normal for any intelligent person to vote for him. However, the nationalistic parties joined together and made some joint declarations to the effect that they did not have enough freedom in the former system, so they managed to influence people in that way. And the people in the Balkans are rather primitive, if I may put it that way. They knew exactly what had happened during the Second World War, and their opinion was reflected in the results of the elections. And there was nothing that could be done after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelic, did you register this party in Sarajevo with the court?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: The party was registered in Sarajevo on the 26th of June during the -- 26th of September, I apologise, in Sarajevo during the constitutional assembly. There were people who were in charge of that. They registered the party there, and we registered our branch in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please help us understand something that I'm not clear on. Did you indicate that this party did not participate in the multi-party elections at all?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No. It participated in the first multi-party elections, but it gained very few votes. I believe 11 per cent or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the national parties of the HDZ, the SDS, and the SDA, what other parties appeared on or in the multi-party elections, please, if you could name a few?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: The socialist party participated in the elections under the leadership of Zeljko Radisic, then the HDZ -- well, I have mentioned then. Then the liberal party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the non-participation or potential non-participation of persons associated with this party was based on discriminatory factors or simply on strict percentages for a very low result in the multi-party election?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Because of a very low results mostly, but you have to be familiar with the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be able to judge about what kind of people we are and how it all ended.
