Unfortunately, that was the kind of result that we had, and the situation hasn't changed a great deal. You have seen the results of the latest elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, a little bit about a person you described as your good friend Stjepan Kljujic who was the Croat -- at one time a Croat representative of the presidency, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. He even used to be the president of the Bosnian branch of HDZ. He attended a meeting together with me and Arslanagic, and he wanted me to organise a rally at the stadium belonging to the Borac football club. I believe it was in the wintertime, in November. And we managed to organise this rally which was not held because of some problems, some conflicts with the SDS that occurred in the meantime. Later on, he lost his favours with Franjo Tudjman and withdrew from the party and established a new party recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "lost his favours with Franjo Tudjman," would it not be more correct to say that he did not agree with the extremist nationalist anti-multi-ethnic approach that the HDZ had taken on. He was not a person who would tolerate that. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: We were not in a position to discuss -- we did not have an opportunity to talk, the three of us, Arslanagic, himself, and me. Everything happened very fast. I didn't see him for a while, and then I heard him on the telephone. He said, "I have lost my position with Zagreb," and then all connections were cut off. Later on I heard some news to the effect that he helped some members of the Serb community in Sarajevo which was under siege at that time, and -- but you are probably right in saying that he was -- he didn't agree with the policy of Franjo Tudjman and that that is the reason why he lost his position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was your last contact with him, either personally or through any other means?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: It was before an international tournament in Sarajevo three years ago when the local authorities didn't let us attend the tournament, so I tried to contact him so that he could exert his influence so that we would be able to participate in the tournament. However, it was Minister Karalic, I think, who sent a very cunning letter to him saying that he had nothing against our participating in the tournament; however, that letter was never sent to us. We were only informed by that over the telephone, but we could not go there without that particular piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: The Borac club didn't go there and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you, please, are you aware, where did Mr. Kljujic spend the entire period of the war? Where was he physically located during the entire period of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: During the war, as far as I know, he was in Sarajevo. He was hiding in a shelter in a basement. This is what a good friend of him told me, a person by the name of Vukajlovic. He was the manager of the Bosna basketball club who died in the meantime. He was the one who protected him in Sarajevo, and he told me that Kljujic was in Sarajevo, hiding himself in one of the shelters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow any of the activities of the government in Sarajevo during the war to know if perhaps this was true or not true? True that he was in Sarajevo, true that he never abandoned Sarajevo, but did you check to see whether or not he may have been out and about?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was no chance for me to do that. There was a war on. We couldn't go to Sarajevo and there were no communications. But one would hear these things. I'd go to Belgrade. Somebody would come and say -- this was just hearsay, and it is on the basis of that I am giving you this statement. Whether that is correct or not I'm not sure, but that is as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you've said today, it appears that the principal attraction of this reformist movement or alliance, if we want to talk about it later as that, was its economic programme. Would that be fair to say, its economic programme?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you articulate any aspect of its programme about either human rights or inter-ethnic relations in Bosnia? Can you talk about that? Is there anything that sticks in your mind about the platform of that party or movement on those issues?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I couldn't talk about these ethnic things, but I know that when he came into power, the things he said, and whatever he said came true. Inflation, hyper-inflation, was checked, the dinar became convertible. He went to America to ask for aid and he got it, as well as from the European Union. He told us --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Who do you --

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I mean Ante Markovic. I mean Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did he ever articulate to you or anyone -- did you know him? Did you know Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Once we were introduced at Dzevad Haznadar's, in his enterprise. Kecmanovic was there. Ante Markovic was there. We talked about these things, we made agreements, and then everyone went his way, that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the Kecmanovic that fled to Belgrade? Is this the person we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Dr. Nenad Kecmanovic who fled to Belgrade. He's back in Sarajevo now. He's a commentator on the television station of Republika Srpska. He's a respected person there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understanding that it was principally the economic aspect of this party or movement, are you suggesting or do you want us to understand that a person who espoused or supported the principles of this movement could not possibly support the principles of a national party or movement? Are they mutually exclusive, in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. That party had nothing to do with the nationalist movements. Those are at least my assumptions, because whatever was agreed was achieved, so we had no reason not to trust him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Could a person, in your opinion, support either an all-Serb or all-Croat or perhaps even an all-Muslim entity and still think that the ideas of Ante Markovic were sound and made sense?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Among educated people, everyone said that Ante Markovic's was the best and that he should be supported. And he proved that. When it all fell apart, he didn't join any of the nationalist parties. He continued to work on his own, and afterwards he was even an advisor to the Macedonian government. So he had a good programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Mr. Markovic supported the breaking away of the Serb municipalities to form the Republika Srpska? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you for a little bit of assistance, and in order to do that, I'm going to ask the usher to show you several documents which have been provided. The newest of the documents have been provided to Defence counsel. The other documents are in the binders which were admitted in 1999 as Prosecution exhibits, and I will refer --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you can start -- if you have a packet to present to the witness, it would be very helpful. While this is being done, the numbers of the new exhibits are 3/1.77 and 3/1.78. They are documents reflecting signatures concerning Red Cross, Geneva Conventions material. The other documents are 2/2.11 to 2.12B as in "boy" and 2/2.14. The latter three mentioned are from the 1999 collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you to take a quick look, please, at the documents on the ELMO, if it's possible to put them on the ELMO. 2/2.11. 2/2.11. The document is both in English and in Serbo-Croatian. This is a document, Mr. Bijelic, dated 22nd of June, 1992. This document -- MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. Bijelic testified about his role in the establishment of the Reformist Party. He was the manager of a sports club, and he worked on the affirmation of the party, the Reformist Party. Mr. Bijelic, who is a player, having played 800 matches, and a manager, is being shown documents of the Crisis Staff of the region of Krajina that the reformist forces have absolutely nothing in common. So this question has nothing to do with the questions testified to by Mr. Bijelic today. These are documents from 1992. He was testifying about 1990, after which all his activities ceased in connection with the reformist forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course, applying the relevance test, any political knowledge that may or may not be possessed by this witness is critical to the Court's assessing his credibility and his ability to convey to this Court whether or not anything Kvocka may or may not have undertaken is a legitimate reflection of political interest or commitment. These documents are very relevant inasmuch as they discuss the essence of who represents Serb people as a whole. It doesn't talk about Serb people who believe in certain -- I apologise to the interpreters, I'm speaking too quickly. I think the relevance of all the documents which I have presented that are in evidence already, and just I'm asking for comment I'm not asking for admission therein, merits comment by this witness so the Chamber can know how he thinks about the political situation in BH. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may add a sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only for the credibility of the witness, Ms. Susan Somers, because these documents are outside the date reviewed because the witness testified about 1990 and this is 1992. So solely for the purpose of impeaching the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, please, to take a look at this document which is signed by Radislav Brdjanin on behalf of the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I see Mr. O'Sullivan on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My learned friend has said this document is signed by an individual. I don't believe there's any evidence in the record of the authenticity of this document or the signature of the document. If that has been established, then perhaps we can proceed with these questions; and until that happens, in my submission, counsel's testifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour? These documents are admitted into evidence. One can always look at weight if there's any question of authenticity. But as admitted documents, I would like to ask to proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you, please, to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. These documents were admitted under which conditions or circumstances? I don't remember. Could you remind us, please, Ms. Susan Somers, and could you also remind the parties. Maybe the Defence does not remember either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I can -- excuse me, Your Honour. I have been helpfully informed by Mr. Saxon, they were admitted subject to challenges of authenticity by the Defence. In fact, no such challenge had been at the time of admission rendered, and they appear to be in. However, Your Honour, whether or not the signature, if I may -- the point is, at this point the content, because there are several documents with the same phrase, and I think the repetition perhaps may be evidence of the intent behind the phrase, that it was not a random comment thrown into a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan made a sign as if he wanted to intervene. Do you still wish to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Documents are admitted under Rule 89 (C) as a matter of relevancy. Now, questions of authenticity go to weight. When there's no proof here as to authenticity, and my learned friend is making submissions regarding authenticity of this document and putting it to the witness that certain aspects of this document have been proven, and in my submission they have not been proven. We don't know the providence of these documents; we don't know who signed it; we don't know whether the witness knows anything about this document. So as much foundation as not been laid, and in my submission it's improper for my learned friend to make submissions when there's no evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, if I understand correctly, you wanted to test the credibility of the witness. If the witness hasn't signed this document, you can ask him a question that you have to ask him without putting the document to him, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that would be difficult, Your Honour, because although the issue is weight, and certainly during our rebuttal case if there is a challenge to documents, we can address that in our rebuttal case, but in terms of if -- even if the Chamber only looks at it for weight, it is important that it is seen that it is from a document that purports to be an official document. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Ms. Susan Somers, you could say "I know that," and then put your question. You yourself have said that you were going to use the document for that purpose only, so it is not necessary to link the information you have with this document. And we will see what the response of the witness will be, whether the witness knows or does not know how to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As long as the Chamber understands that I am not testifying that when I say that "I know that." I am reading, in fact, from a document that is before -- has been before the Chamber for a period of time. And again, we would ask for its admission -- well, it is admitted, but if there is a challenge to authenticity, to allow us to read the passage, because I think it is the phraseology that is important, and my paraphrasing it will not serve the same purpose as reading it. And again, if weight is the issue, the Chamber is within its province to weigh that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we will have to decide on that. But Mr. Krstan Simic first, let us hear you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I add a single sentence. I have a feeling that my learned friend wishes the witness to comment on the document. I would first like him to be asked whether he ever saw the document, whether he knows of its existence, and we have an expert witness, Nenad Kecmanovic, who can comment on documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, show the witness this document and ask him whether he knows it, and then put your question to him. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelic, this document before you, you may or may not have seen; is that correct? You may not have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No, but let me help you. This -- it is dated 1992, and in 1992 I was in Belgrade with the Borac handball club until 1995. We competed there. So I know nothing at all about this, nor does it interest me. My activities ceased after the elections. We left and went to Serbia, or to be quite specific, we were stationed in Obrenovac, the Srbija Hotel there. You can check that with the handball association of Serbia. And I was in the Palace Hotel in Belgrade until 1995, and this can easily be checked. And I don't know what happened in the meantime, so there's nothing more I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to Banja Luka, I presume was the place to which you returned in Bosnia, had you been aware that the position of the government, at least up till a point in time when the war ended, was that -- which is articulated in decision point one where it says the, "Serbian Democratic Party," that would be SDS, "is the sole representative of the Serbian people." Had you been made aware of that position?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No. Let me say again, I am not a politician. My main interest was to assert the Borac handball club because changes had occurred, major changes. After a single-party system, a multi-party system was introduced, and we couldn't find our way around. Borac as a club also took a step forward, and that is what guided us. So I never even read this document. As soon as I saw the date, I saw that I had nothing to say because Borac was a Yugoslav club. It was a member of the Yugoslav league. You can check the names of the people involved, and I headed those lists. To make things worse, there were no telephone connections, even, so we couldn't know many things. Especially in Serbia in those days, one couldn't learn about these things. You know why: The press was censored. All we wanted was to keep the club alive, and the handball association of Yugoslavia welcomed us, and we thanked them for this, even though we came from another state. And all that I can say, I can say about what happened until elections in 1991. When we didn't succeed, I gave up. I went back to Borac. Borac had survived, and it exists to this day, and I know nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About Borac, was it a state-run, state-funded club? Was it an asset of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No. No. Borac was founded as an association of citizens. Ten citizens get together and form a club. And that is how we were financed, as an association of citizens. The state had nothing to do with us. However, our results were such that the state showed an interest and it assisted us. Not financially, but our players would more easily get jobs upon graduation. As top-level sportsmen, they would be given apartments. In that sense, the state assisted us, but not in any other way. We belonged to an association of citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: Did Borac bring economic benefit, fame, notoriety, to both Yugoslavia and now to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Not economic benefit. Football players and basketball players bring economic benefit. Handball is a poor man's sport. He didn't gain those funds. Even when we compete in Europe, we have to pay to be able to participate as opposed to football and basketball. But in the case of handball, that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that members of this club are given a certain respect, a certain deference?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, that quite certainly. Yes, we did enjoy respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about the membership of your party, and I'd like to throw some names out to you, please, and see if you might be able to comment. Dragan Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, he was a member of that party. Then he left it and joined the SDS, and now he's President of the parliament of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when he left the party?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Immediately after the elections. He changed his mind. He went to Belgrade, then he came to Banja Luka, and so on. As far as I know, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not to spend too much time on this, just to put in front of you very briefly 3/1.77 and 3/1.78. They are in English only. I apologise. That is the language of the document. Do you see it in front you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is it possible to put it on the ELMO? It might be easier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is a document that was compiled at the invitation of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva on the 22nd of May, 1992. It concerns various aspects of the conventions, and the representatives of various persons or parties from Bosnia-Herzegovina are there. The second name is a Mr. D. Kalinic, representative of Mr. Radovan Karadzic, President of the Serbian Democratic Party. Would be this the same Mr. Kalinic about whom you were just speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I assume it is the same man. Because immediately after the elections when he saw the SDS party had won, he joined them. So I assume it is the same man because I don't know any other Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is this document which also bears the identifier of Mr. Kalinic, and it was for that purpose that he was once a member of your party and subsequently became a representative of Radovan Karadzic that I show this to you. It is not necessary to discuss it any further. Can you tell me, please, who was a man named Pavic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Marko Pavic? He was Minister in Dodik's government. Minister of Transportation, as far as I know. He is from Prijedor. If that is the one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also a member of your party?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I don't remember, because in Prijedor it was not formed. Whether he was a member of a party somewhere else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he ever worked with Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I think -- I assume that when Biljana formed her party that he joined that party, but it is an assumption on my part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the following names, I'd like to ask you perhaps if you can tell us about. Excuse me for looking. Burho Kapetanovic. Does that sound familiar to you? A Muslim. Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Where is he from? No. Is he from Doboj perhaps? I know a Kapetanovic from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there several Kapetanovics in your party?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I can't remember, because there were five or six representatives enrolling people. There were quite a number of Muslims. There were quite a number of Croats, and quite a number of Serbs or, rather, Yugoslavs, especially people from mixed marriages. They all declared themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a Mehmedalija Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a Rizah -- sorry. I can't even read my own writing. How about a Croat named Miroslav Turnusek? Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know Miroslav Pitrosek. He's the coach of the women team of Vrbas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aleksandar Komsic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't know where this is leading. Mr. Bijelic was a manager working on the promotion of the party. He didn't keep records. There were records by municipalities, and I don't know how Mr. Bijelic can be expected to know all the members of the reformist forces in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, but the witness can say whether he knows or not. Are you afraid that he cannot answer those questions? He can answer them. I was going to say to Ms. Susan Somers that your time is about to end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have another one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: I don't mind, Your Honour. I'll tell you whatever I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this was Aleksandar Komsic.

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These names are persons who were in the Reformist Party in your area who ended up in Omarska camp. Did you ever get any type of request for assistance? Are you aware of any type of request for assistance that may have made it through, as it were, the network of fellow former party members to help out to get these people out of the camps?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: You see, it was impossible for me to know that because I said I was active until the elections, and since we didn't win, I withdrew and concentrated on Borac. Tosic, a former Partizan football player from Prijedor, apparently Partizan pulled him out of the Omarksa camp, I think it was. As for the others, I don't know because the party virtually no longer existed. I went to Belgrade and I don't know anything any more. Since we didn't win, the party dissolved, this unfortunate war started, the non-Serbs were forced out of the Banja Luka just as the Serbs were forced out of Sarajevo, and no one could really keep track of all that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Ms. Susan Somers. Mr. Simic, any additional questions? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] In view of the time, I shall have just two questions, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bijelic, when you spoke about the programme of Mr. Markovic, can you tell us whether he had already started with the privatisation process and the introduction of the market economy in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes. It happened in Banja Luka. The major companies were about to be privatised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question for you. The reformist forces of Mr. Markovic, were they in favour of multi-ethnicity? Did they want to become involved in that? Was that one of their objectives?

utterances.speaker: MIRO BIJELEC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of their objectives. It was a precondition for their success. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. I don't think that we have any questions for you, Mr. Bijelic, so I can only thank you for coming here to testify and to wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence and a lot of success in your work. Let me ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] See you tomorrow at 9.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
